attachment.content:
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

content.content: {"result":"{\"success\": true, \"data\": {\"path\": \"/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0509_12/projects/simgate-modular-routing/paper_framing.md\", \"content\": \"# Paper Framing — simgate-modular-routing\\n\\n## Target Venue\\n- Primary: EMNLP 2026 Main (ARR short paper, 4 pages + references)\\n- Fallback: EMNLP 2026 Findings\\n- Deadline: ARR May 25, 2026 (11 days remaining)\\n\\n## Core Insight\\n\\nLLM agents on rule-governed environments face catastrophic failures from hallucinated state transitions. Deterministic external computation (environment simulators, code interpreters) eliminates these failures — but what exactly does routing learn? We introduce episode-level counterfactual analysis (per-step oracle labeling degenerates to 97.4% ties in sparse-reward settings) and discover that **death avoidance accounts for ~90% of routing signal** on ScienceWorld (Δ_full=+29.60 [A], Δ_nd=+2.84 [A], DAF=90.41% [A]; Pearson r=0.9698, p=8.12e-07 [A] across 11 task types / 245 episodes [A]; source: plan-012-full). Non-death performance difference is small but non-negligible (Δ_nd/Δ_full=9.6% [A]). Key exception: find-non-living-thing (n=40, zero deaths, Δ_full=+9.58, all non-death performance difference) [A]. The contribution is the empirical finding (death avoidance dominance) + the diagnostic methodology (episode-level counterfactual labeling), not the router architecture itself.\\n\\n## Core Claims (2 claims for short paper)\\n\\n**C1 (Death avoidance dominates routing signal)**: On ScienceWorld, deterministic simulation dramatically outperforms LLM reasoning (Δ_full=+29.60 [A]), with **death avoidance as the dominant mechanism** (90.41% of the performance gap [A], measured by Δ decomposition; plan-012-full, 11 tasks / 245 eps [A]). Episode-level label distribution: det-preferred 86 / internal-preferred 9 / no-preference 150 (out of 245 episodes) [A]. Death rates: internal 42.9% / deterministic 16.3% [A]. Non-death score deltas are small but non-negligible (Δ_nd=+2.84 [A], 9.6% of Δ_full [A]). Key exception: find-non-living-thing (n=40, zero deaths, Δ_full=+9.58, all non-death performance difference) [A]. Pearson r=0.9698 (p=8.12e-07) [A] between per-task death rate difference and Δ_full across 11 task types [A]. The value of deterministic computation in interactive environments is concentrated in catastrophic failure prevention, not positive task guidance.\\n\\n**C2 (Episode-level counterfactual labeling as diagnostic methodology)**: Per-step oracle labeling degenerates in sparse-reward environments (97.4% tie rate on ScienceWorld). Episode-level counterfactual analysis — running complete episodes under pure-internal and pure-deterministic strategies — overcomes this circularity and reveals the death-avoidance mechanism. The resulting labels train a lightweight router (Qwen3-1.7B) that serves as a **diagnostic probe** for LLM failure modes. [Hypothesis, pending plan-005]: the router may learn within-task-type early warning signals of catastrophic failure from early observations, beyond simple task-type classification.\\n\\n**D013 note**: C1 no longer claims \\\"selective > unconditional.\\\" Router training (plan-002/003) proceeds — if router ≈ always-det, that IS the finding; comparison with rule-based baseline (plan-011) quantifies whether learned routing adds value over keyword heuristics.\\n\\n## Positioning vs Tool-Use Literature (Dream-driven addition)\\n\\n**Critical gap identified by all 3 Dream tiers**: The core pipeline (counterfactual labels → SFT small classifier → selective invocation) is standard in tool-use learning. Must position against:\\n- **Toolformer** (Schick et al. 2024): Self-supervised tool-use learning via API call insertion. SimGate differs: hindsight labels from environment forking (not self-supervised), safety-aware framing (not general tool selection).\\n- **ART** (Paranjape et al. 2023): Automated tool selection via LLM reasoning. SimGate: dedicated lightweight router, not LLM-as-router.\\n- **Chameleon** (Lu et al. 2024): LLM-as-planner routing to diverse tools. SimGate: single modality (deterministic computation), explicit small router.\\n- **ToolkenGPT** (Hao et al. 2024): Token-level tool triggers. SimGate: step-level routing with counterfactual labels.\\n\\n**Our differentiation**: (1) Episode-level counterfactual labeling — overcomes per-step oracle circularity in sparse-reward environments (97.4% tie rate), providing ground-truth episode outcomes rather than tie-break artifacts. (2) Empirical finding: death avoidance accounts for ~90% of routing signal [A] — quantifies WHERE and WHY tool invocation helps (catastrophic failure prevention, not positive guidance). (3) Diagnostic framework — counterfactual analysis + router as probe reveals systematic LLM failure modes across task categories. (4) The contribution is the finding + methodology, not the router architecture — this distinguishes from \\\"we built a better tool selector\\\" papers.\\n\\n**Paper must include a dedicated Related Work section** (not just intro paragraphs). Minimum coverage: tool-use learning (Toolformer, ART, Chameleon), adaptive computation (CogRouter, ARES, Mixture-of-Depths), world model routing (ITP-R, Dyna-Think), agent frameworks (ReAct).\\n\\n## Story Spine\\n\\n- **Problem**: LLM agents hallucinate state transitions on rule-governed environments (temperature physics, chemical reactions), leading to catastrophic failures. ITP-R routes to an approximate LLM world model but underperforms pure internal reasoning (62.58 vs CogRouter 84.6 on ScienceWorld). ReTool/AgentMath learn when to invoke code interpreters but use implicit routing entangled with the backbone. Tool-use learning methods (Toolformer, ART, Chameleon) learn general tool selection but don't specialize for catastrophic failure prevention or use counterfactual trajectory labeling.\\n\\n- **Our framing**: We use episode-level counterfactual analysis to understand WHAT routing learns. Per-step oracle labeling degenerates (97.4% tie rate on ScienceWorld), so we run complete episodes under pure-internal and pure-deterministic strategies, comparing episode-level outcomes. Key finding: ~90% of routing signal is death avoidance [A] — deterministic computation's value is almost entirely concentrated in preventing catastrophic failures (-100 penalties). Non-death performance difference is small but non-negligible (Δ_nd=+2.84, 9.6% of Δ_full [A]). A router trained on these labels becomes a diagnostic probe for LLM failure modes, but (per D013) is structurally limited to task-level risk classification under episode-level labels.\\n\\n- **Headline result template**: \\\"Episode-level counterfactual analysis across 11 ScienceWorld task types (245 episodes) [A] reveals that death avoidance accounts for 90.41% of routing signal [A] between internal LLM reasoning and deterministic computation (Δ_full=+29.60, Δ_nd=+2.84 [A]; r=0.9698, p=8.12e-07 [A]). We propose this analysis as a diagnostic methodology for understanding when and why tool invocation helps LLM agents.\\\"\\n\\n## Paper Structure (4-page short paper)\\n\\n| Section | Pages | Content |\\n|---------|-------|---------|\\n| Abstract | 0.2 | Counterfactual analysis framing, death avoidance finding, headline numbers |\\n| Introduction | 0.8 | Problem (LLM catastrophic failures) + gap (per-step oracle degeneracy) + contribution (empirical finding + methodology) |\\n| Method | 1.0 | Episode-level counterfactual labeling (why per-step fails: 97.4% ties → episode-level solution); router training as downstream application; death decomposition analysis framework |\\n| Experiments | 1.5 | Death avoidance decomposition (core) + router vs baselines (always-det, rule-based, learned) + routing pattern analysis figure |\\n| Conclusion | 0.3 | Summary + limitations (episode-level granularity, single benchmark) + future (step-level labeling, MATH) |\\n| References | ~0.5 | Not counted in 4-page limit |\\n\\n## Anticipated Reviewer Concerns & Mitigations\\n\\n1. **\\\"Novelty is incremental — just SFT a small model to classify\\\"**\\n   - Mitigation: Contribution is the empirical finding (death avoidance mechanism + routing patterns) more than the architecture. Router-as-diagnostic-probe reveals systematic LLM failure modes. Explicit vs implicit ablation quantifies the gap.\\n\\n2. **\\\"Only one benchmark (ScienceWorld)\\\"**\\n   - Mitigation: Short paper format justifies focused evaluation. ScienceWorld uniquely tests rule-governed dynamics with catastrophic penalties. Discuss MATH/API extension as future work.\\n\\n3. **\\\"Comparison unfair — CogRouter uses RL (CoPO), you use SFT\\\"**\\n   - Mitigation: Our primary comparison is SimGate vs ablated baselines (always-internal, always-deterministic, random, heuristic) — all same training budget. CogRouter/ITP-R cited from papers for context.\\n\\n4. **\\\"Death avoidance is trivial — just always use deterministic\\\"**\\n   - Mitigation: We do NOT claim selective > unconditional deterministic. Our contribution is the empirical finding that death avoidance dominates routing signal (~90% [A]), and the methodology that reveals this. Always-deterministic is a strong baseline — the interesting question is WHY (death avoidance), not WHETHER to route selectively. Plan-011 rule-based comparison + plan-012 death decomposition quantify this.\\n\\n5. **\\\"DAgger gap — SFT on pure-strategy trajectories may not transfer to mixed-strategy deployment\\\"**\\n   - Mitigation: Acknowledge explicitly (cite Ross et al. 2011). Plan C exacerbates this: router trains on always-internal/always-deterministic trajectories but deploys on mixed. Report train/test gap. If significant, discuss DAgger-style iterative relabeling as extension. Note: Plan C's episode-level labels avoid oracle circularity (no per-step tie-breaking), which is a methodological advantage even if distribution shift remains.\\n\\n6. **\\\"ScienceWorld's -100 penalty inflates gains\\\"** (Dream all 3 tiers)\\n   - Mitigation: Report gains WITH and WITHOUT death episodes separately. If non-death gains are small, honestly acknowledge that the primary value is catastrophic failure prevention — this IS our framing. Also report: what fraction of routing labels are genuine vs tie-break artifacts.\\n\\n7. **\\\"Missing tool-use literature — this is just Toolformer\\\"** (Dream all 3 tiers, CRITICAL)\\n   - Mitigation: Dedicated Related Work section. Position against Toolformer/ART/Chameleon. Differentiation: counterfactual trajectory labeling (not self-supervised), safety-aware framing (not general tool selection), explicit modular router (not LLM-as-router). (4) Episode-level counterfactual labeling — overcomes per-step oracle circularity in sparse-reward environments (97.4% tie rate).\\n\\n8. **\\\"Rule-based routing baseline missing\\\"** (Dream median + worst)\\n   - Mitigation: **D014 resolved — keyword routing structurally fails.** Two keyword lists tested: v1 (generic verbs incl. connect) → ≈always-det (85.8%); v2 (science-only: heat/boil/melt/freeze) → ≈always-internal (4.9%, near-zero hits). - **ToolkenGPT** (Hao et al. 2024): Token-level tool triggers. SimGate: step-level routing with counterfactual labels.
